comparablesNote: No Tester profile: Claude picked these comparable games for this run: PBS KIDS mazes, ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles), Monument Valley, A Maze Race.

comparables.title: PBS KIDS mazes
comparables.compare: Onboarding style, spoken instructions, idle hints, and failure tone for a pre-reading 5-7 audience
comparables.why: Same core genre (character-led simple maze) but built specifically for pre-readers with full voice-over and idle hints — directly targets mazle's biggest flagged gaps (no audio, no idle-stuck hint, text-only controls panel).

comparables.title: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
comparables.compare: Grade/age-banded difficulty structure and instruction wording length
comparables.why: Same genre (path/maze puzzles) explicitly organized by school grade with short audio+text instructions, useful to benchmark mazle's 25-word controls panel and single-level, no-ramp structure against a graded difficulty model.

comparables.title: Monument Valley
comparables.compare: Wordless onboarding and no-fail, affordance-driven design
comparables.why: Not a kids-marketed game but the reference genre's best example of teaching a 3D path-finding game with zero reading required and no punishing fail state, contrasting with mazle's text-heavy controls overlay and spike-reset failure.

comparables.title: A Maze Race
comparables.compare: Maze-size progression and multi-level ramp versus a single fixed maze
comparables.why: Same core maze-navigation genre and web-playable like mazle, but structured as a sequence of growing mazes — useful contrast since mazle currently has only one level with no difficulty ramp beyond it.

summary: Mazle already nails the fastest-win fundamentals for this genre — a single clear goal, instant low-cost retry, and a calm non-scary hazard shown by shape not color — but it is the only comparable game here with zero audio and a text-only, 25-word onboarding panel, both of which directly block pre-readers in the 5-7 bracket and fail the accessibility/usability checks (R16, idle-hint target, 5-word max). The highest-leverage fixes are small and fit a lightweight three.js game: a 3-6 word spoken instruction, a visible pause/mute/quit icon, an idle-stuck hint, and trimming the controls panel to icons. Lower-priority polish — a second/third maze for a difficulty ramp, a star on finish, and hiding the debug FPS/Position overlay — would round things out once the audio and reading gaps are closed.

compared_with: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
items.they_do: PBS KIDS has a known character speak the goal aloud with a replay-voice button so nothing depends on reading; ABCya pairs a handful of words with audio narration scaled to grade level.
items.we_do: Level 1 opens straight into play with a 25-word text-only controls overlay (WASD/arrows, strafe, mouse look, touch drag zones) that a 5-7 year old needs read to them, and there is no audio at all.
items.suggestion: Add one speechSynthesis/WebAudio line, e.g. "Use the arrows, find the door!" (5 words), played once when Level 1 starts, with a small speaker-icon button to replay it, and shrink the on-screen text to match.

compared_with: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
items.they_do: Both are built so a child can always get back out or replay instructions without help — PBS KIDS lets kids replay voice lines, and neither traps a child on the play screen.
items.we_do: The playing screen has no visible pause/mute/quit control at all (automatic check: rule R16 fail); only developer debug panels are shown.
items.suggestion: Add one icon-only button (top corner, ~48px touch target, no text) that pauses and offers "Home"/"Play again", satisfying R16 without adding any reading burden.

items.they_do: PBS KIDS shows an idle hint — a nudge, glow, or voice line — if a child pauses too long, tuned for younger players.
items.we_do: Automatic checks flag no in-play hint when stuck; a 60s+ idle period currently triggers nothing, versus the ≤20s target for this bracket.
items.suggestion: After ~15s of no movement, glow or arrow-highlight the next correct corridor (reusing the maze solver already used by the bot), optionally paired with a short "this way!" audio line.

compared_with: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
items.they_do: ABCya's Pre-K/K puzzles keep on-screen text to a handful of words backed by audio; PBS KIDS needs no reading at all.
items.we_do: The controls panel is a 25-word block, five times the 5-word max for this bracket, shown as a permanent overlay for the whole level.
items.suggestion: Replace the WASD/arrow text with 2-3 simple drag-direction icons (e.g. a hand-drag glyph over screen-left, an eye/look glyph over screen-right) and drop the keyboard-key text for the touch path used by this bracket.

compared_with: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
items.they_do: Both use continuous light music/sound effects and voice-over throughout play, plus a cheer sound on success.
items.we_do: 0 audio files, no WebAudio, no speechSynthesis — completely silent, including on the spike hit and the "You found the way out!" win screen.
items.suggestion: Add two short WebAudio cues: a soft "boop" on spike contact paired with the existing instant reset, and a 1-2s cheer/chime when the door is reached on the win screen.

items.they_do: A Maze Race ramps maze size gradually across many levels, each finishable in 1-3 minutes, giving kids repeated wins with rising challenge.
items.we_do: Only one 29x29 maze exists (34-cell solution, 8 dead ends); kid-persona runs already win 100% in a median 53.95s with nowhere to go afterward.
items.suggestion: Reuse mazeCarver.js/levels.js to generate 2-3 smaller follow-on mazes (e.g. 11x11, 15x15, 21x21) as Levels 2-3, keeping the same single-hazard rule, so a session has a natural next step instead of stopping after one level.

compared_with: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
items.they_do: ABCya gives a checkmark/cheer/brief animation and unlocks the next puzzle on completion; PBS KIDS sometimes awards stickers.
items.we_do: Winning shows only the text "You found the way out!" and a "Play again" button — no stars, points, collectibles, or unlocks.
items.suggestion: Award one star automatically on every finish (never scored on speed or mistakes) and show it on the win screen, rewarding finishing rather than perfection.

items.they_do: Monument Valley teaches entirely wordlessly via glowing, tappable handles; PBS KIDS uses a character that points or speaks instead of showing text.
items.we_do: Onboarding relies solely on a static 25-word text overlay rather than any in-play demonstration of the drag-to-move gesture.
items.suggestion: On Level 1 only, play a 2-second animated hand/arrow glyph over the first corridor demonstrating the drag gesture before input is required, then fade it out.

items.they_do: PBS KIDS uses large touch targets and standard mobile-friendly viewport behavior that doesn't fight a parent trying to help.
items.we_do: The page's meta-viewport disables pinch-zoom (axe moderate warning), preventing a parent from zooming in to help a child with any remaining text.
items.suggestion: Remove user-scalable=no / maximum-scale=1 from the viewport meta tag so pinch-zoom works normally.

compared_with: ABCya logic games (maze and path puzzles)
items.they_do: Both show only child-relevant UI on the play screen (goal/progress), with no developer instrumentation visible to the player.
items.we_do: A persistent debug FPS/Position box stays on screen alongside the controls and level-name panels, adding visual clutter with no value to a young player.
items.suggestion: Gate the FPS/Position debug box behind a ?debug=1 query flag so it only appears for developers and the play screen stays uncluttered for kids.

present.evidence: goals_and_rewards: "One goal per level: find the door" — a single, simple objective once the child is in the maze.
core_loop: touching the spike resets the player to the start; difficulty_curve notes fail cost is low with 0-1 fails per kid run in bot data, no menu interruption.
goals_and_rewards: winning shows "You found the way out!" with a "Play again" button that waits for input; no autoplay into another level.

present.pattern: Forgiving/non-scary failure design (hazard shown by shape not color)
present.evidence: accessibility: "hazards are shown by shape not color alone"; art_and_audio describes the spike as a simple "grey spike cone cluster", not a threatening design.

missing.pattern: Sound on every tap / celebration on every success
missing.suggestion: Add a short WebAudio chime on reaching the door and a soft cue on spike contact; currently 0 audio files and no WebAudio/speechSynthesis exist.
Trigger a glow/arrow hint after ~15s idle, well under the current 60s+ with-no-hint state flagged by automatic checks.
Introduce a small friendly character or arrow guide near the start that points toward the first corridor, since onboarding currently has no character or voice at all.
Replace the static 25-word text overlay with a brief animated gesture demonstration on Level 1 before requiring input.
Award a star automatically on every level finish, shown on the win screen, since there are currently no stars, points, or collectibles.

missing.pattern: Gentle difficulty ramp / natural progression across levels
missing.suggestion: Add 2-3 additional smaller mazes as later levels so difficulty ramps gently instead of stopping after the single existing 29x29 maze.

Add wall-slide/collision smoothing to movement — kid-persona runs already bump into walls 11.5 times/min versus a near-optimal solver bot, suggesting collision handling is stricter than it needs to be for small hands.

profile.onboarding: No menu or tutorial; Level 1 opens straight into play with a controls panel (25 words: WASD/arrows, strafe, mouse look, touch drag zones) shown as an overlay the whole time. No taps required before play starts (taps-to-play check passed) but reading the controls text needs a 5-7 year old to be read to.
profile.controls: Keyboard W/↑ forward, S/↓ back, A/← strafe left, D/→ strafe right, mouse to look; touch play drags the left side of the screen to move and the right side to look, with no on-screen buttons.
profile.core_loop: Walk the 3D maze corridors, avoid the spike trap, and reach the exit door; touching the spike resets you to the start and you re-walk the path.
profile.goals_and_rewards: One goal per level: find the door. Winning shows "You found the way out!" with a "Play again" button; no stars, points, collectibles, or unlocks (bot run: kid persona 5-7 win rate 100% over 3 runs).
profile.difficulty_curve: Single 29x29-cell maze (perfect maze, 34-cell solution, 8 dead ends) with one spike hazard placed in a dead end only 3 cells from start, on-solution avoidable; fail cost is low (instant reset to start, 0-1 fails per kid run in the bot data) but there is no ramp beyond this one level.
profile.game_feel: Software-rendered fps averaged 37.6 (p95 frame 66.6ms, one spike to 466.6ms), no haptic/audio feedback on movement or the spike hit; solver bot finished near-optimally (99% of optimal path) while kid-persona runs bumped into walls often (11.5 bumps/min).
profile.art_and_audio: Low-poly pastel 3D (sky-blue walls, green floor, grey spike cone cluster, brown door with light-blue windows); 0 audio files, no speechSynthesis, no WebAudio — completely silent.
profile.session_length: Kid-persona (5-7) bot runs: median time to first win 53.95s, range 45-168s across 3 seeded runs, well within a 5-10 minute session; only one level exists so there's no continued session beyond that.
profile.usability: Automatic checks flag no in-play hint when stuck (idle 60s+ with no hint, target is ≤20s) and no visible pause/mute/quit controls on the playing screen (R16 fail); the persistent debug FPS/Position box is developer instrumentation with no value to a young player and adds visual clutter alongside the controls and level-name panels.
profile.accessibility: Text has good contrast (light text on dark boxes, brown/white "Play again" button) and hazards are shown by shape not color alone; but the controls text is a 25-word block above the 5-word max for this bracket, there is no spoken/audio version of any instruction (loudness check fails this bracket), and the page's meta-viewport disables pinch-zoom (axe moderate warning).
profile.ads_and_purchases: None seen; network check found only 2 same-origin requests and no analytics/tracker globals.
profile.notes: Biggest gaps for 5-7: missing pause/mute/quit control (fails rule R16), no audio/spoken instructions at all, and a text-heavy controls panel that a pre-reader can't parse alone — flagged by both the automatic checks and Claude's content review, despite play itself being fast, low-fail, and non-scary (spike is a simple grey cone, reset is instant).
